metadata.name: ss
metadata.displayName: ss - Another utility to investigate sockets (modern replacement for netstat)
metadata.description: Another utility to investigate sockets (modern replacement for netstat)

installation.note: ss is part of the iproute2 package, which is installed by default on modern Linux systems

overview.summary: The ss command is a modern replacement for netstat that displays socket statistics. It's faster, more efficient, and provides more detailed information than netstat. ss directly queries the kernel for socket information, making it the preferred tool for network socket investigation on modern Linux systems.

syntax.description: ss displays socket information. Without options, it shows all established connections. Various filters can be applied to show specific socket types, states, or addresses.

options.use_case: See which ports are listening for connections
Faster output without DNS/service name resolution
Identify which process owns each socket (may require root)
Show both listening and non-listening sockets
Show hostnames instead of IP addresses

examples.title: List all listening ports
examples.description: Show all TCP and UDP listening ports with numerical addresses
examples.output:
Netid  State      Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
tcp    LISTEN     0      128     *:22                  *:*
tcp    LISTEN     0      128     127.0.0.1:3306         *:*
examples.use_case: Check which ports are open and accepting connections

examples.title: Show connections with process info
examples.description: Display listening sockets with process names and PIDs
examples.output:
Netid  State      Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port  Process
tcp    LISTEN     0      128     *:22                  *:*                  users:(("sshd",pid=1234,fd=3))
examples.use_case: Identify which programs are using network ports

examples.title: Show socket summary
examples.description: Display summary statistics of all sockets
examples.output:

UDP:   89

examples.use_case: Get quick overview of network socket usage

examples.title: Show connections to specific port
examples.use_case: Check if a specific port is in use

examples.title: Show memory usage
examples.description: Display memory usage for each socket

misconceptions.title: Same as netstat
misconceptions.reality: ss is faster and more efficient than netstat, and provides more detailed information. It's the modern replacement.
misconceptions.tip: Prefer ss over netstat for better performance and more features

misconceptions.title: Requires installation
misconceptions.misconception: ss needs to be installed separately
misconceptions.reality: ss is part of iproute2, which is installed by default on modern Linux systems
misconceptions.tip: ss should be available out of the box on Ubuntu and most modern distributions

common_pitfalls.description: Process names not displayed without proper permissions
common_pitfalls.solution: Use 'sudo' with '-p' option to see process information

common_pitfalls.description: Output can be overwhelming with many connections
common_pitfalls.solution: Use filters like 'state established' or 'sport :PORT' to narrow results

common_pitfalls.description: ss has different syntax than netstat
common_pitfalls.solution: Learn ss-specific filters and options. Use 'ss --help' for full syntax

related_commands.description: netstat is the older tool that ss replaces, but still widely used
lsof -i can also show network connections and processes
ip command from iproute2 package handles routing and interfaces
iftop shows real-time network bandwidth usage

best_practices: Use 'ss' instead of netstat for better performance
Combine '-tuln' for comprehensive listening port information
Use '-p' with sudo to identify processes using ports
Use filters like 'state established' to narrow results
Pipe output to 'grep' to filter specific ports or addresses
performance_tips: ss is significantly faster than netstat because it queries the kernel directly
Use '-n' flag to skip DNS resolution for faster output
Filters are processed efficiently by the kernel, making ss very fast even with many connections

additional_notes.modern_tool: ss is the modern, recommended tool for socket investigation, replacing netstat
additional_notes.kernel_direct: ss queries the kernel directly via netlink, making it faster than netstat which reads from /proc
